title: Food delivery
brief: You run food delivery in a few big cities. People browse menus, pay for an order, and watch a courier move on a map. Dinner time is brutal, and the payment company sometimes slows down. Nobody may be charged twice, and no paid order may vanish.

clarify.q: How fresh must the courier dot on the map be?
clarify.a: Within a few seconds. Couriers send a position every 4 to 5 seconds.

clarify.q: What if the payment company is slow?
clarify.a: Orders still need to be taken. Tell the customer the payment is pending and finish it when the service is back.

clarify.q: Can a customer see an old order status after paying?
clarify.a: No. Right after placing an order the customer must see it.

notes: Use the payment share to estimate order rate. Card data stays with the payment company.
Dinner peak is about 5,000 requests a second. Courier pings are 26 percent of traffic (approx.).
Notification speed measures provider acceptance. Device receipt is outside this traffic model; check expiry, provider outcome and retries in the correctness trace before claiming delivery guarantees.

numbers.label: Courier pings per second at peak
Servers for 5,000 req/s at about 1,000 req/s each
numbers.how: 5,000 / 1,000 = 5, plus one spare so a zone can fail

hints: A payment company that slows to 3 seconds will fill your servers with waiting requests. What can stop that?
Set a short timeout on the payment call and add a circuit breaker, so your servers fail fast instead of waiting. An idempotency store makes a retried payment safe.
Tracking freshness and financial durability need separate resource and failure boundaries. Measure the failed boundary, waiting time and retry work before choosing a change.

editorial.summary: Three kinds of traffic share one app: menus (cacheable), courier dots (a steady stream of tiny writes) and payments (rare, must be exactly once). Give each its own treatment and put a fuse on the one call you do not control.

designs.name: Fused payments, cached menus, fast positions
designs.why: A circuit breaker and a short timeout keep a slow payment company from tying up every server. The idempotency store makes retries safe. Menus come from a cache. Courier positions go to a store built for many small writes. Notifications wait in a queue.

tradeoffs: A 1 second payment timeout fails some slow-but-fine payments. In exchange your servers keep serving menus during a payment slowdown.
Sync replication on the order database costs a few milliseconds per write and means a failover loses nothing.
Courier positions use a store that can lose the very latest ping. Losing one ping is harmless; losing an order is not.
Notifications through a queue can arrive seconds late and never block ordering.
Running 6 servers instead of 5 costs about $140 a month and lets a zone fail without a brown-out.
editorial.realWorld: Delivery apps handle a few hundred thousand orders on a busy night in a large country, with courier positions updated every few seconds (approx.).

correctness.prompt: The payment provider times out after accepting a charge. What idempotency key and payment state transitions would make a second tap safe?
correctness.discussion: Use a stable key for the logical payment, not a new key for each attempt, and bind it to the payer, amount and currency. Enforce uniqueness and store pending, succeeded and failed states durably. A timeout leaves the outcome unknown, so reconcile with the provider using the same key rather than start a fresh charge. Apply callbacks conditionally so a late failure cannot overwrite success. Record the order update and its outbox event together; a cache lookup followed by a charge leaves a race. One business order must span mobile retries. Cross-service work needs explicit recovery; compensation is an operation that can also fail. Tracking freshness and financial durability need separate resource and failure boundaries.

fields.label: Step 1. Order F payment times out. What does a second tap do?
options: Create a second order and charge
Resume F and reconcile its original payment key
fields.explanation: One business order must span mobile retries.

fields.label: Step 2. The restaurant rejects F after payment succeeds. What follows?
options: A durable compensating refund or void state with retryable operation ids
Delete F and forget the payment
fields.explanation: Cross-service work needs explicit recovery; compensation is an operation that can also fail.

fields.label: Step 3. Courier positions arrive late during dinner traffic. What is shown?
options: Use newer position versions, isolate tracking load from paid-order commits
Block paid orders until every position catches up
fields.explanation: Tracking freshness and financial durability need separate resource and failure boundaries.

correctness.responsibility: Coordinate a paid order and restaurant acceptance without duplicate external effects.
correctness.limits: The traffic model does not execute this protocol. The checked trace covers its central responsibility; the written explanation is retained for review.

twist.brief: Demand has settled at about 1,250 requests/s. The new monthly ceiling is $8,061. The original burst reserve now competes with the operating budget. Decide which reserve to keep, then test its failure headroom. All data and recovery promises still apply.

design.name: Smaller workload, measured reserve
design.why: Reduce the paid floor for the quieter workload, preserving the required copies and recovery settings. This design was checked through the full event day.
